notes.1: Surprisingly this was a challenging question with many of the candidates appearing not to understand the term validation check. The Examiners gave three examples to act as scaffolding to help candidates with their answers. The type of answer we expected were length check, range check and check digit.
notes.2: This question was quite well answered with most candidates gaining at least three marks.
notes.3: Overall this question was quite well answered although part (b) was challenging for some candidates.
notes.4: This question was quite well answered with many candidates able to give some good answers, gowever part (a) was more challenging than part (b).
notes.5: This was a challenging question for candidates. It looked at the differences between a cloud-based laptop and a laptop that contained an SSD. Most answers that gained marks concerned the need or not for the internet, and the difference in storage amounts available to the two different laptops. Some candidates wrote answers that related to hacking, but this was not a difference as both systems could be hacked. The batter answers related to the size of storage and the fact that once bought the laptop with SSD did not have any other storage costs whereas the laptop that used the cloud had to pay monthly for storage.
notes.6: This was a challenging question with few candidates understanding the concept of a computer model. Many believed that it was an actual model bridge and composed their answers accordingly. Correct answers generally centred around the concepts of safety and costs. Even though these candidates gained marks for these answers few candidates were able to explain why these were important. For the prose questions candidates need to give reasons or expansions to their answers in order to achieve good marks.
notes.7: This was a very challenging question for most candidates especially in part (a) which was a new topic for the examination.
notes.8: Most of this question was quite challenging for the candidates, with only part (b) gaining good marks.
notes.10: As a whole this question was quite challenging for the candidates.
notes.key_messages: This paper due to the issues with Question 9a was in line overall with previous sessions but as six extra marks were added to all candidates it looked on paper to be slightly easier compared with other examinations in this series.The paper showed a very good range of marks with the men mark in the high 20s. The range was fairly evenly spread between 6 and 49 marks. The paper covered a large range of topics, some new ones and some that had been seen on previous examination papers, therefore giving a good coverage of the syllabus. The balance included technical questions as well as more general questions. This year’s paper had less marks available than in previous papers, reducing the marks to 80 rather than 100. As the scenarios of the paper change it is important that candidates read the question carefully before answering it as marks are awarded for answering the question that has been set. Candidates who performed well in this paper used specific and detailed language when answering the prose questions. To a lesser extent than in previous years some candidates answer the comparison questions using a split answer of advantages and disadvantages, with a line drawn down the answer lines. This type of layout does not give enough scope to gain high marks as the answers are simply statements without a comparison. As with previous series I need to report back on the lack of use of generic names for hardware and software. There has been an increase in the number of candidates using brand names to answer the questions. It is clearly stated on the front page of the examination paper ‘No marks will be awarded for using brand names of software packages or hardware systems. As with previous reports I need to report again on candidates who write extra parts of answers elsewhere in the paper. Occasionally candidates may need to expand their answers on to other parts of the examination paper or onto extra sheets. It is important that if this occurs the candidate clearly writes where the extra part is written and writes the question number on the extra work. The paper is marked electronically and if the candidate writes on extra sheets or on the blank pages/spaces in the examination paper the extra elements or key points within it may be missed. There has been an increase this year on candidates using extra space but not clearly noting which question this refers to. There has also been an increase in the candidates who use extra sheets when there is space below the question to continue with the answer.
notes.general_comments: There is an increasing trend of candidates missing out answers to questions and therefore not attempting an answer. Sometimes attempting an answer may result in answers being correct. The paper gave all candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge and understanding of ICT using a wide variety of topics. When a question indicates a specific number of answers, candidates should only write one answer in each allocated space as only one is marked for that space. Any extra answers placed on the same line or below the numbered responses are ignored. Candidates need to be clear in the answers given rather than using basic statements like it is quicker. A good rule of thumb it to add ‘because’ and then give a valid reason. All answers on the paper should relate back to the question being set. In several cases, handwriting was quite difficult to decipher. Examiners spend time trying to decipher words where the writing is not clear but candidates do risk their answer not gaining marks where handwriting is undecipherable.
notes.2a: The answer to this question was section break but the Examiners allowed page break as an alternative answer. This may not be the case in future series.
notes.2b: Image file format was generally well understood with most candidates gaining marks here.
notes.2c: Footers were well understood by the majority of the candidates, and most were able at least to give an example of what was contained in a footer.
notes.3a: Most candidates were able to specify appropriate display formats. Some found the question challenging and tried to write data to go into the boxes rather than the type of format.
notes.3b: This part of the question was quite challenging for many of the candidates. Most candidates knew that a QR code would redirect a user to a website, however fewer candidates could describe how this could happen by writing ‘with my phone’ rather than with a ‘device with a camera’. Candidates understood that a QR code contained information about the product and saved space on the packaging.
notes.3c: The correct formula or an explanation as to why it was wrong was well answered with most candidates gaining marks. The Examiners allowed other variations to BODMAS.
notes.4a: This was a challenging question although there were some good answers concerning the user ID and password. Most candidates could distinguish between user IDs and passwords and also understand their purpose. The user ID gives access to the computer system whilst the password protects the data. Many candidates knew the User ID was unique, but some also thought that the password was also unique. Some candidates quoted that it would be a combination of both the user Id and password that would make the login details unique.
notes.4b: Biometric methods were well understood by many of the candidates. The question asked for examples of biometrics i.e. fingerprint for examples, but we were lenient with candidates that gave the device i.e. fingerprint scanner. However some candidates gave examples that were not appropriate to the question, and these did not gain credit.
notes.7a: Extended reality is a mixture of virtual reality and augmented reality. Few candidates gained marks on this question as they described virtual reality rather than extended reality.
notes.7b: This topic had been set previous and candidates then were able to gain good marks, however candidates found this question was more challenging than in previous examination series. Candidates knew what a 3D printer was and how it operated but could not relate this to industrial processes and the reasons that 3D printers were a good idea or a bad idea. Some candidates wrote that 3D printers worked faster than a human carrying out the task and that they could work all night. However, candidates could have gained marks by stating that if there had been a power outage or a fault in the programming then no one would know until it was too late. There was a misconception that 3D printers produced perfect models but did not add that it depended on the program. Some candidates correctly stated that the 3D printer could only work with some materials and that they produced fewer parts, and their initial cost could be high. This was one of the harder questions on the paper and candidates had to analyse the use of 3D printers giving both positives and negatives.
notes.8a: This was a challenging question with candidates explaining the concepts concerned with the internet working or not and this affecting the smart security system. Some candidates thought that if the internet connection failed then the system would go off, rather than the owner not being able to monitor it.
notes.8b: There were some good answers to this question with the concepts of sensors used in a security system being understood by most candidates.
notes.8c: This question which was related to the ANPR system was generally well understood and some good answers were seen. Some candidates did not fully read the question and thought the system had to do with road safety. Some candidates however thought that the CCTV camera was in some way the intelligent body and did not envisage any connected computer system or database.
notes.8d: Some sensible problems that could occur to stop the number plate being read were seen. However with some of the answers seen this session some candidates do not give the full explanation or reasoning behind their answers. For example some candidates rightly stated that ‘it may confuse numbers and letters’ without explaining why this would be the case. Others stated that the number plate could not be reads if it was dirty or the weather conditions were bad without expanding on the answers given.
notes.9a: Due to an error on the number of lines for this question the examination board decided that all candidates should receive the maximum 6 marks.
notes.9b: This was a challenging question with candidates still having issues with the topic. This time the question placed the examples associated with corporate house style in part (b). Many candidates mixed up house style and making documents look professional. Some candidates however gave correct answers that related to consistency of the webpages and that if corporate house style was used then the webpages could be linked directly with the University.
notes.9c: Surprisingly the features of house style were not well known. Candidates understood the features of the corporate house style could be colour and font or even logo. But they did not expand upon these answers only giving one-word answers and therefore marks could not be awarded the marks. Stating the position of the logo or the size of the logo would have achieved the marks. The answers the Examiners were looking for were font style or font type and background colour etc.
notes.10a: (i), (ii), (iii) The difference between interview, observation and questionnaires was known by many candidates. In place of interview some incorrectly used words like ‘communication’, ‘conversation’ or ‘dialogue’. Parts (i) and (ii) were well answered but in (iii) candidates wrote answers like surveys which is too vague an answer.
notes.10b: This was a challenging question even though it was a standard question. Few were able to correctly identify items that needed to be designed after the systems analysis. INFORMATION AND
